---
title: "Mixtures of frontier reports"
subtitle: "2.11 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 16 and 19"
description: "Randomisation over complete reports at a specified mean disclosure."
---

Randomisation between two complete reports can attain intermediate points on the error–disclosure frontier. At a
specified mean number of stated pairs, the diamond gives the mixture's expected wrong count. The square gives the
smallest error count among single reports at that disclosure, when such a report exists. The randomisation applies
to the entire grade report, preserving coherence in each realisation. Its mean disclosure and mean error describe
the distribution over reports rather than a further deterministic grade vector. The examples compare unrestricted
and restricted report families.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Six sites, mean 10.** The mixture selects the report stating 12 pairs with probability .50 and the report stating 8 pairs otherwise.
  The average error count is .01714. No single report states exactly this mean number of pairs: the diamond describes
  an average over reports rather than a new grade vector.
- **Six sites, mean 9.** The more-disclosing report now has chance .25. The mixture expects .01332 wrong directions;
  the best single report at this disclosure expects .1597, a gap of .1464. The square and diamond share the same horizontal coordinate.
- **Six sites, mean 12.** The selected point is a corner with .02477 expected wrong directions: no mixture is needed.
  Moving the mean-disclosure slider changes the lottery, while moving the withholding cost changes the supporting
  line and its best report.
- **Four units, mean 4.** With two criteria, the quantities are expected **weighted** wrong directions. The mixture
  has 19/40 against the best single report's 7/10, a gap of 9/40. Its two complete reports each have chance 1/2.
- **At most 3 grades, mean 9.** The family has 603 reports and ends at 12 stated pairs. The unrestricted endpoint
  conclusion is **not guaranteed for this family**. The fixed-order example below gives a different reason that a
  restricted family can miss the unrestricted endpoint.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The half-cost endpoint requires the full report family and no latent ties on positive-weight criteria. The small
fixed-order figure uses its own restricted boundary; it is not the unrestricted boundary. The six sites and finite
laws are supplied examples, rather than fitted empirical posteriors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank)
g <- list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=2,F=2), c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=3,F=3))
vapply(g, function(x) postrank_evaluate(x, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.20)$E[1], numeric(1))
```

This evaluates the two complete reports at the mixture's endpoints. Their error counts appear in the vertex table;
randomising those reports forms the average point.
:::
